docs.title: AtlasMind: Production AI Assistant
docs.text:
Summary

Type: Personal project - live production system Stack: Python, FastAPI, pgvector, vLLM, Groq, AWS Bedrock, Oracle Cloud A1

Key outcomes:

  • Live at atlasmind.de - fully deployed and running
  • 5 runtime-switchable LLM backends (Ollama, vLLM, Groq, AWS Bedrock, OpenAI-compatible)
  • Self-healing query retry loop: up to 4 automatic correction cycles per failed JQL query
  • Two-stage router that bypasses the JQL parser for general conversational queries
  • GPU inference on OCI A1 Flex (Ampere ARM) at zero egress cost

docs.title: Challenge
docs.text:
Jira's JQL query language is powerful but inaccessible to most stakeholders. Writing correct JQL requires knowing field names, operators, function syntax, and project-specific custom fields - knowledge that resides with a handful of engineers and not with the people who need reports.

The goal was to build a system that converts plain-English requests ("show me all open FPGA blockers assigned to Alice since last sprint") into valid, executable JQL - and recovers automatically when it gets the query wrong.

docs.title: Approach
docs.text:
Built a two-stage routing architecture:

  1. Intent classifier - determines whether the user's query needs JQL or is a general question (documentation lookup, Jira how-to). General queries bypass the JQL pipeline entirely and go straight to the LLM with RAG context.
  2. JQL generation + self-healing loop - for query requests, the LLM generates JQL from the user's prompt. If Jira's API returns a validation error, the error message is fed back to the LLM as additional context, and the query is regenerated. Up to 4 retry cycles before the loop exits with a graceful error.

The RAG layer uses pgvector to store and retrieve Jira field definitions and project metadata, keeping the context window small and the queries accurate.

LLM routing is runtime-switchable across 5 backends with no restart required, enabling cost-performance tradeoffs on the fly: local GPU inference for low-latency, Groq for speed, AWS Bedrock for compliance-sensitive queries.

Deployed solo on an Oracle Cloud A1 Flex instance (Ampere ARM architecture) using Docker Compose, with Tailscale for secure tunneling and zero-cost ingress.

docs.title: Qt/C++ CAN Hardware Simulator
docs.text:
Summary

Type: Tooling project - automotive Head Unit development Stack: C++, Qt Framework, CAN Bus

Impact:

  • Physical tool cost per developer seat eliminated: USD 5,000-14,000 → $0
  • 1,000+ automotive test cases parallelized and run overnight
  • Test cycle moved from hardware-dependent sequential runs to parallel CI execution

docs.title: Challenge
docs.text:
Development and testing of an automotive Head Unit required physical CAN bus hardware interfaces - proprietary tools costing between USD 5,000 and USD 14,000 per developer seat. This created two problems:

  1. Access bottleneck: The number of developers who could run tests simultaneously was capped by hardware availability. Test execution was sequential and hardware-dependent.
  2. CI/CD incompatibility: Automated overnight test runs were not feasible because they required physical hardware to be attached and available.

The project had a test suite of 1,000+ automotive test cases that needed to run reliably and frequently, but the physical hardware constraint made this impractical.

docs.title: Approach
docs.text:
Reverse-engineered the vehicle Head Unit's hardware communication behavior and built a software CAN simulator in Qt/C++ that faithfully replicated the hardware interface at the protocol level.

The simulator intercepted CAN frames at the software boundary, processed them through the same state machine logic the physical hardware would execute, and returned the expected responses. From the perspective of the test suite, the simulator was indistinguishable from the physical hardware.

Key aspects:

  • Protocol-level fidelity: CAN frame structure, timing behavior, and response sequences matched the physical hardware precisely enough to run the full test suite without modification
  • Qt framework: Used Qt's event loop and signal/slot mechanism to manage concurrent CAN channel simulation
  • CI integration: With no physical hardware dependency, the simulator ran in standard Linux CI environments, enabling overnight parallel test execution across multiple agents

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Hardware tool cost per developer seat: USD 5K-14K → $0
  • 1,000+ test cases parallelized across CI agents and run overnight unattended
  • Development teams no longer blocked on hardware availability for test execution
  • Test coverage increased as running tests became low-friction

docs.title: GPT-2 Transformer From Scratch
docs.text:
Summary

Type: Personal research project Stack: Python, PyTorch

Scope:

  • Custom byte-pair encoding (BPE) tokenizer
  • Multi-head causal self-attention from first principles
  • Feedforward sublayers, layer normalization, residual connections
  • Weight initialization matching OpenAI's GPT-2 paper
  • Full training and evaluation loop

docs.title: Challenge
docs.text: Reading papers and using pre-built transformer libraries gives a working model but not a deep understanding of how it actually works. The challenge was to build a complete GPT-2 implementation from scratch - no HuggingFace Transformers, no shortcuts - to internalize every component at the implementation level.

docs.title: Approach
docs.text:
Implemented the complete GPT-2 decoder-only architecture in Python from the ground up:

  • Tokenizer: Custom byte-pair encoding (BPE) implementation, building the vocabulary merge table from scratch and handling the encode/decode cycle
  • Attention: Multi-head causal self-attention with separate Q/K/V projection matrices, scaled dot-product attention, causal masking (upper triangular), and output projection
  • Transformer block: Combined attention sublayer + feedforward sublayer (two linear layers with GELU activation), each wrapped with pre-layer normalization and residual connections
  • Full model: Token embeddings + learned positional embeddings, stacked transformer blocks, final layer norm, and unembedding projection to vocabulary logits
  • Training loop: Cross-entropy loss on next-token prediction, gradient accumulation, learning rate scheduling

The implementation followed the original GPT-2 paper (Radford et al., 2019) and Andrej Karpathy's nanoGPT as a reference cross-check after the initial build.

docs.title: Results
docs.text: Functional GPT-2 architecture that trains and generates coherent text. The primary outcome was depth of understanding: every hyperparameter (n_head, n_layer, n_embd, block_size) has a clear mechanical meaning from having built the code that uses it.

docs.title: Netra MCP: Confluence and Jira Read/Write Server
docs.text:
Summary

Type: Open-source tool - Atlassian automation for AI assistants Stack: Python, FastMCP 2.0, httpx (async), Pydantic, Docker, Cloud Foundry

Key outcomes:

  • 10 MCP tools across Confluence and Jira, usable from Claude Desktop, VS Code Copilot Agent mode, and any MCP-compatible client
  • New (Oct 2026): Jira read and write - read and search issues, clone a template ticket into up to 50 issues, bulk-create, and edit fields
  • Every write tool defaults to dry_run=True: nothing changes until the user says "apply it"
  • Confluence pages edited in their native ADF JSON at exact paths - no regex anywhere
  • Deployed on Cloud Foundry as a shared server; each user's own Atlassian token travels per request, so page history and Jira audit logs show the real person
  • 268 tests, 95% coverage on the Jira package, ruff and mypy --strict clean

What's new: Jira read/write support

The server started as a Confluence page editor. Two releases in October 2026 extended it to Jira:

  • Write (clone_jira_issue, create_jira_issue, edit_jira_issue): clone a template ticket and set each summary from a pattern, create tickets in bulk from a file in your workspace, or change fields on one issue. All three preview every item before writing.
  • Read (get_jira_issue, search_jira_issues): read a ticket in plain language - description as text, custom fields by display name, links, sub-tasks, recent comments - or run a JQL search with extra columns. Lets the AI check a template before cloning, verify the clones afterwards, and review a ticket's readiness.

docs.title: Challenge
docs.text:
Release work on Atlassian tools is full of repetitive, error-prone edits. A release report in Confluence can hold dozens of Jira macros, each with a JQL query pinned to a version string. Moving to the next release means hand-editing every macro, every date, and every version token, then hoping none were missed. On the Jira side, each rollout means creating the same ticket again and again - one per service or variant - by cloning a template and retyping the summary.

AI assistants can describe these changes easily but had no safe way to make them. A tool that writes to shared team pages and project backlogs has to be predictable: show exactly what will change, never touch the wrong node, survive a teammate editing the same page, and act as the real user rather than a shared service account.

docs.title: Approach
docs.text:
Confluence: structure-aware edits, not text substitution

The server reads pages as ADF (Atlassian Document Format), the JSON tree Confluence stores internally. A walker tracks the exact path to every node; an inspector extracts every JQL query with its location; a replacer applies longest-match-first rules scoped to the right macro parameters, protects @mentions, and regenerates macro IDs on clones. A validator checks the structure before any write, and a differ produces a grouped change log for the dry-run preview. Version conflicts (someone else saved the page) are retried with exponential backoff.

Jira: bulk operations that are safe to re-run

The Jira extension adds an async JiraClient that mirrors the Confluence client - typed errors per status code, HTTP 429 retries honouring Retry-After, and network retries only on idempotent calls, never on a POST whose response was lost.

  • Clone and create handle 1-50 issues per call. Fields are copied from the template's create screen with an exclude list, override keys accept a field ID or its display name ("Service Name"), and missing required fields return VALIDATION_FAILED before any write.
  • Idempotent re-runs: summaries that already exist in the project are marked SKIPPED_EXISTS, so after fixing one failed item the whole batch can be run again and only the missing issues are created. Partial failures return a PARTIAL status with one result per item.
  • Clones link back to their template with an "is cloned by" link.
  • Read tools render issues for an AI to reason about: ADF converted to plain text, users by display name, custom fields resolved via expand=names, and the 20 most recent comments.

Multi-user by design

On a shared HTTP deployment the server holds no Atlassian identity of its own. Each tool call carries the caller's email and API token as request headers, and the server builds a fresh client per call. Jira tools use X-Jira-* headers when present and fall back to the caller's X-Confluence-* pair - never mixing pairs, and never reading server environment credentials on HTTP. A structlog processor redacts any credential-shaped log field as a backstop.

docs.title: OpenFlowBI: Open-Source Jira Flow Metrics
docs.text:
See how work really flows through your Jira projects - how long tickets spend in each status, where they wait, and how many get finished each week - in dashboards you host yourself, for free.

OpenFlowBI started with one question: can the flow metrics teams buy eazyBI for be built entirely from free, open-source parts? This project is the answer.

  • The questions

    How long does work sit in review? Where does it wait? Is the team finishing more, or just closing smaller tickets? The answers live in Jira's change history.

  • The cost

    eazyBI answers these questions well. It is also a paid app, licensed by the number of users on the whole Jira site - not by how many people read the dashboards.

  • The alternative

    OpenFlowBI rebuilds the same core metrics from Jira's history using only open-source tools, on your own machine. Free, MIT-licensed, and yours to change.

Summary

Type: Open-source tool - free alternative for Jira flow metrics (September - October 2026) Stack: Python, dlt, PostgreSQL, Cube, Apache Superset, Docker

What you get:

  • Cycle time, time in status, and throughput, rebuilt from every issue's complete change history
  • No licence and no per-user cost - MIT-licensed open source
  • Your Jira data stays in your own Postgres database
  • Works with Jira Cloud and Jira Server / Data Center
  • Incremental sync: after the first load, each run fetches only what changed
  • One-script install, with a ready-made demo on Apache's public Jira - no account needed to try it

docs.title: Why eazyBI was the reference
docs.text:
I build delivery dashboards in eazyBI, and for Jira flow reporting it sets the standard. Its key move is importing each issue's change history and turning it into measures such as days in transition status. That is exactly what flow metrics need: not where a ticket is now, but how long it spent everywhere along the way.

The catch is the licence. On Jira Cloud, eazyBI's price tier follows the user count of the whole Jira site. A site with 2,000 users pays at the 2,000-user tier, even if only a handful of delivery leads open the dashboards. There is a 30-day trial but no permanent free tier.

So the direction for OpenFlowBI was clear: keep eazyBI's proven model - import the history, choose the fields, define the measures once, explore in dashboards - and rebuild it with open-source building blocks.

docs.title: eazyBI concepts, open-source building blocks
docs.text:
If you know eazyBI, you already know how OpenFlowBI works. Each familiar step has an open-source counterpart:

In eazyBI you... In OpenFlowBI Built with Import Jira issues with change history flowbi extract pulls issues and their full changelog, incrementally dlt, PostgreSQL Choose which custom fields to import flowbi fields shows how often each field is actually filled in, then you promote the ones you want Versioned decision log in Postgres Analyse the Transition Status dimension and days in transition status One row per status period for every issue, starting at its creation SQL transform Work with a cube of dimensions and measures A semantic model that defines each measure once, exposed as a single flow view Cube Build reports and dashboards Point-and-click charts and dashboards in the browser, no SQL needed Apache Superset Pay a licence per Jira user Free MIT licence 
flowchart LR
    J[Jira\nCloud or Server/DC] -->|import history| E[Extract\nissues + changelog]
    E --> P[(Your Postgres)]
    F[Choose fields] --> P
    P --> T[Time in status\nper issue]
    T --> C[Cube\nmeasures defined once]
    C --> S[Superset\ndashboards]

docs.title: An honest comparison
docs.text:
OpenFlowBI is not a feature-for-feature replacement for eazyBI. It covers the flow-metrics core - and is open about where the mature product still leads.

  • Where OpenFlowBI shines

    • No licence cost, whatever the size of your Jira site
    • Your data never leaves your server
    • Open code you can read, audit, and extend
    • Plain SQL access to the same data, for any other tool
    • Built on widely used open-source components

  • Where eazyBI still leads

    • Years of maturity and vendor support
    • Rich calculated measures (MDX) and time intelligence
    • Change history for many fields - OpenFlowBI models status history today
    • Many data sources beyond Jira
    • Ready-made report templates and gadgets inside Jira
    • Per-user access control (on the OpenFlowBI roadmap)

docs.title: Under the hood
docs.text:
Turning Jira's history into trustworthy numbers is harder than it looks. Four problems shaped the design:

  • History records transitions, not state. An issue's first status never appears as a transition, so each issue's timeline is anchored at its creation date. Without this, every first status period would silently disappear.
  • Changelogs come back in pages, through three different APIs. The extractor uses the embedded changelog when it is complete, falls back to the bulk endpoint (up to 1,000 issues per request), then to per-issue paging - and flags any issue whose history is incomplete.
  • Jira Cloud search lags behind recent changes. Each sync re-reads a one-hour overlap window, so late-indexed updates are never missed, and duplicates merge away.
  • Real instances have 200+ fields, most of them empty. Field discovery samples up to 5,000 issues and measures fill rates, so the choice of columns is based on data and recorded in a versioned log.

The project follows a "build nothing that already exists" rule: dlt handles pagination and loading, Cube the semantic layer, Superset the dashboards. Hand-written code is limited to what is specific to Jira.

  • An end-to-end CI check that migrates a fresh database, starts Cube, and queries the flow view
  • A written architecture review hunting specifically for silent wrong numbers: all six critical findings fixed, each with a regression test

docs.text:

  • Row-level security, so each user sees only their own projects
  • Prebuilt images on a public registry
  • Deployment beyond a single Docker Compose host

docs.title: S-Band Telemetry Waveform Product
docs.text:
Summary

Type: Product development - aerospace/defense Stack: C, FPGA, RTOS

Outcomes:

  • LDPC encoder/decoder implemented on FPGA from M.Sc. research baseline
  • Complete MAC layer and HAL software stack developed
  • Product secured recurring aerospace defense contracts

docs.title: Challenge
docs.text:
Develop a production S-Band telemetry waveform product for aerospace/defense use. The waveform required a high-performance LDPC (Low Density Parity Check) forward error correction layer to meet link budget requirements in challenging RF environments.

LDPC codes are capacity-approaching - they perform close to the Shannon limit - but their hardware implementation is non-trivial: the iterative belief-propagation decoding algorithm requires careful architecture to achieve the necessary throughput on FPGA with acceptable resource utilization.

docs.title: Approach
docs.text:
Led product design across two layers:

FPGA - LDPC encoder/decoder

Implemented the LDPC encoder and belief-propagation decoder directly in FPGA logic. The implementation drew on M.Sc. research (see below) in hardware channel coding, adapting the academic decoder architecture for production constraints: fixed-point arithmetic, pipelined throughput, and resource budgeting for the target device.

Embedded software - MAC/HAL stack

Developed the complete MAC (Medium Access Control) layer and HAL (Hardware Abstraction Layer) software stack in C on an RTOS. The software stack managed framing, timing, synchronization, and the interface between the application layer and the FPGA waveform core.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Complete S-Band telemetry waveform product delivered
  • Recurring aerospace defense contracts secured
  • LDPC implementation from research → production, demonstrating the direct path from M.Sc. work to shipped hardware

docs.title: Research
docs.text:
M.Sc. Thesis: Hardware Implementation of Optimum Channel Codes

School of Electrical and Electronic Engineering, Nanyang Technological University, Singapore - 2011

Investigated Low Density Parity Check (LDPC) codes: capacity-approaching block codes whose iterative belief-propagation decoding algorithm outperforms most existing forward error correction schemes. The thesis covered code construction, hardware decoder architecture for FPGA implementation, and performance characterization under AWGN channel conditions.

The research formed the direct academic foundation for the FPGA-based LDPC implementation in the S-Band telemetry product above.
